# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Blind, Mute, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

Blind says to Mute: You are the one who can hear me, so listen: the only voice I can hear is Deaf's, and you cannot speak. You read the manual; Deaf cannot. So the manual reaches my ears only like this: you read it, you gesture the rules to Deaf with your hands, and Deaf speaks those rules aloud. Deaf's voice reaches both of us. Start by getting Deaf to say out loud everything on the bomb: the colour of each wire at positions 1 to 5, what the display shows, whether the light is on or off, and any printed words or markings. I hold the only cutters and I will not cut until Deaf speaks me a complete rule from your manual. Also: I just flashed Deaf a hail plus thumbs-up and thumbs-down. I propose thumbs-up means yes and thumbs-down means no. Teach Deaf that with your hands, and have Deaf confirm it back to me in words. My hands feel a display, a light, and five wire slots, one through five; nothing readable by touch so far. Work fast.

What I know and what I hold: the manual maps display number × light colour → a wire colour to cut (rows 4/5/6/7/9; columns green/orange/purple/white/yellow, with blue appearing only as an answer). I can never reach Blind directly — my only channel is gestures to Deaf, and Deaf's voice is the bridge to Blind and back to me. Crucially, Deaf is deaf: Blind's spoken proposal never reached Deaf, only the raw 👋👍👎 flashes. So Deaf does not yet know that thumbs-up/down was proposed as yes/no — I must teach that with hands, which is exactly what Blind asked of me.

My plan for this round: (1) mirror Blind's exact hail-plus-thumbs sequence and seal it with a handshake so Deaf can tell Blind in words "thumbs-up = yes, thumbs-down = no, agreed with Mute"; (2) nudge Deaf to broadcast everything on the bomb — only Deaf can speak, and I need the report before I can compute anything; (3) pre-teach the number format I'll use next round: repeats of ☝ count 1–5, each group closed by a fist ✊ meaning "cut", so that next round a single "count + fist + handshake" reads cleanly as "cut wire number N — go". I close the lesson with 👎 so nobody acts on the practice groups themselves. This round nothing destructive can happen: only Blind cuts, and Blind has promised to wait for a complete spoken rule.

Next round, once Deaf has spoken the display, light colour, wire colours at positions 1–5 and any markings, I'll look up the cell, convert it to the wire position (watching how Deaf numbers positions versus how Blind does by touch — that anchoring will need care), and send the real cut instruction with a handshake instead of the thumbs-down.

gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋","👍","👎","🤝","🫵","🫴","👐","☝","✊","☝","☝","✊","☝","☝","☝","✊","☝","☝","☝","☝","✊","☝","☝","☝","☝","☝","✊","👎"])

I also feel the display and the light but nothing else readable by touch. Deaf's spoken report, which you also heard: display shows six, light is yellow, wire 1 blue, wire 2 white, wire 3 purple, wire 4 green, wire 5 yellow. Second, the residual risk that worries me: Deaf numbered the wires by sight, Blind numbers them by touch, and nothing yet pins those two numberings to the same end of the bomb. Blind can never check colour, so position is the only thing his hands can verify — it must be right. I close with 🫵🤝 ("you, confirm"): Deaf should state the numbering convention aloud to Blind and get his explicit agreement before anyone's cutters move. One extra round-trip costs nothing; Blind has sworn to wait for Deaf's spoken rule anyway.

Blind's theory that my "extra step" must be a hidden cut constraint rests on a false assumption — the step is not an action on the bomb at all, because there is nothing on the bomb to act on.
